clue.text: Appearing optimistic, girl blushed

parts.note: Rose is a girl's name
someone who blushed has coloured up, gone red

explanation.surface: A young woman reddens, seeming cheerful about something.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'girl blushed' look like a separate event, but it simply joins two pieces: a girl's name and a past-tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing the world through tinted spectacles is the idiom for unreasonable cheerfulness, so a hopeful outlook is described this way.

clue.text: Batter attendant in furious aggression

parts.note: to batter is to strike repeatedly, which a ram does
a page is a boy attendant, as at a wedding or court

explanation.surface: Someone beats a servant in an angry assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like cooking or cricket, but here it is the verb to pound, given by a short synonym; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild, violent spree of destruction is a synonym for frenzied, uncontrolled aggression.

clue.text: With child about, blow into town

indicators.note: the word for child goes about, surrounding, the word for blow

parts.note: a son is a child
wind is a blow of air, as a gale blows

explanation.surface: Someone with a youngster blows into a town on a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' and 'into' are link words. The surface suggests a quick arrival; SWINDON is a large town in Wiltshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindon is a large English railway town in Wiltshire, an example of the category named.

clue.text: Be interested to keep in touch with decorative design

indicators.note: one word holds the other within it, keeping it inside like a pen keeps animals

parts.note: to care is to be interested or concerned
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who cares stays in contact over an ornamental pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keep in touch' reads as a stock phrase about staying in contact, but 'keep in' is the container signal and 'touch' is the word kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartouche is an ornamental oval frame or scroll, as round hieroglyphic royal names, so an ornamental motif.

clue.text: Composer's lean sound

indicators.note: the clue asks for something heard, so a word spoken aloud matches another spelling

parts.note: to list is to lean, as a ship does

explanation.surface: A thin composer's sound, as if describing his music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lean' looks like an adjective for slender, but it is the verb to tilt; the 's is 'is', linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the Hungarian Romantic pianist and composer, an example of the class named.

clue.text: A fabulous British supporter

parts.note: fabulous means belonging to fable, mythical; a supporter in heraldry is a beast holding up a coat of arms, here the royal one

explanation.surface: A marvellous fan of Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wonderful patriot; in fact the royal coat of arms has a lion and a mythical horned horse standing either side as supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-horned horse of legend stands on the right of the royal arms, representing Scotland, so it is a heraldic beast from myth.

clue.text: Tending to give laciest creation

indicators.note: a creation is something made anew, so these letters are reworked into a fresh word

explanation.surface: Inclined to be generous with the frilliest new design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creation' suggests a fashion item, but it signals rearranging LACIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stretchy yields under pressure and springs back, so it tends to give.

clue.text: Every assembly takes turn — nothing out of order

parts.note: all can stand for every
a system is an assembly of working parts; after 'every' it is read in the plural
a go is a turn, as in a game

explanation.surface: Each meeting has its turn, with nothing done improperly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every assembly' gives ALL SYSTEMS, the plural forced by 'every'; 'takes' is a link word adding GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from rocket launches, meaning everything is working and ready, so no part is faulty.

clue.text: Chimney support showing more bulges

parts.note: lum is a Scottish and northern English word for a chimney
a pier is a pillar supporting a bridge or arch

explanation.surface: A chimney's base appears to be bulging more.
explanation.walkthrough: LUM is a Scots word for chimney, familiar in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of lumpy describes something with more swellings and protrusions.

clue.text: Chap's in, cooking vegetable

indicators.note: cooking implies preparing and transforming ingredients, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: the 's here supplies an S, giving the plural chaps
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man has come in and is preparing greens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap's in' reads as a man arriving; the letters CHAPS IN are rearranged, signalled by 'cooking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinach is a leafy green eaten cooked or raw, an example of the class named.

clue.text: The way to find a capital doctor?

definitions.text: The way to find a capital doctor?

parts.words: The way to find a capital doctor?
parts.note: a way is a road, and a capital doctor is both an excellent one and one in London

explanation.surface: How do you track down a first-rate physician?
explanation.walkthrough: HARLEY STREET is the London road famous for private medical consultants; 'capital' means both splendid and of the capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The London street lined with private consulting rooms is the address where top medical specialists practise.

clue.text: A nuisance, demonstrated in two ways?

definitions.meaning: shown like this and like that, as one says while demonstrating with gestures

explanation.surface: An annoying person, shown up two ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: 'like so' shows one way, so the repeated phrase shows two.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild euphemism for an annoying person, and literally means this way and that way.

clue.text: Be liable to fall over right foot

indicators.note: the longer word goes over, covering, the abbreviation so it sits within

parts.note: to totter is to sway unsteadily, about to fall

explanation.surface: Someone is likely to topple onto their right foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot' looks like a person's own, but a TROTTER is a pig's foot, eaten as food.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's or sheep's foot, especially as a dish, is called by this name.

clue.text: Way to get one German mug

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A route to obtaining a mug from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' is a link word joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A stein is a large earthenware beer tankard, a kind of drinking vessel.

clue.text: Excavated corniche holds long history

indicators.note: the rearranged word grips the abbreviation inside it
dug up, turned over, so the letters of the word are disturbed and rearranged

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for long, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A coastal road, dug up, reveals a long past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excavated' rearranges CORNICHE into CHRONICE, which 'holds' L. A corniche is a coastal road cut into a cliff.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a factual record of events in order, a written account of the past.

clue.text: Traffic manoeuvre giving you a real fit?

definitions.meaning: a vehicle turning off to the right
right can mean real or proper, as in a right mess, and a turn is a sudden fit or bout of illness

explanation.surface: A driving move that brings on a genuine seizure.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense uses British usage: 'a right turn' is a proper funny turn, a real bout of faintness; 'giving you' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a motorist veers off rightwards, and colloquially a 'turn' is a sudden attack of illness.

clue.text: Spring's sweet

parts.note: a confection associated with the spring festival, read as a spring that is lovely

explanation.surface: Spring is lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as 'Spring is sweet'; really the 's is possessive and the sweet is the chocolate gift of the spring festival.
explanation.definitionFit: The chocolate ovoid given at the spring Christian festival is a seasonal confectionery treat.

clue.text: For example, mass benefit

definitions.meaning: Mass is one example of a church rite
being of use, as in 'at your ...'

explanation.surface: A large-scale advantage, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mass' looks like bulk, but it is the Christian Mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A church rite such as Mass is a religious ceremony, and help or use given is an aid.

clue.text: Old conspiracy I suppressed — some achievement

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: the letter is held down, pressed within the word for a scheme

parts.note: a plot is a conspiracy

explanation.surface: An old scheme of mine was quashed, quite a feat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' is a link word; 'suppressed' puts I inside PLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A bold or daring deed is a feat, a notable accomplishment.

clue.text: Smooths feature of desert

definitions.meaning: the stretches of fine grains that make up a desert

explanation.surface: Polishes a characteristic of arid land.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbing with abrasive paper makes a surface even, and a desert is known for its expanses of grains.

clue.text: One sparkles, taking extremely sharp corner

indicators.note: at its extremes means only the outermost letters of the word are wanted

parts.note: an angle is a corner

explanation.surface: Someone shining as they take a tight bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is a link word; 'extremely sharp' gives the first and last letters of SHARP.
explanation.definitionFit: A spangle is a small glittering piece of metal sewn on clothes, a thing that glitters.

clue.text: Play losing tennis shot, giving game

definitions.meaning: in tennis a shot that strikes the net and falls back loses the point
a team sport played chiefly by women and girls

explanation.surface: A tennis player misses a shot, conceding a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving' is a link. NETBALL is a British court sport similar to basketball.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis ball caught by the net loses the rally, and the name is also a court sport like basketball.

clue.text: Like sleeve of sergeant that's with the band?

definitions.meaning: having bands of colour, read as belonging to a musical band

explanation.surface: A sergeant's sleeve, as if he played in the regimental band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' suggests musicians, but in the second sense it is a strip of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant's arm bears three chevrons, and something with bands of colour is lined in this way.

clue.text: Party around one's castle is a DJ affair

indicators.note: the party word goes around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: a do is a party
one gives I, and the 's stands for is, so together IS
C is taken as an abbreviation for castle

explanation.surface: A party around one's castle features a disc jockey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'castle' looks like part of the party's venue, but it gives the single letter C; 'is' is a link word before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dance night where a disc jockey plays records is a club event built around recorded music.

clue.text: One raising glass to daisy

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a glass to a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising glass' suggests lifting a pane; the answer is one who proposes a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone proposing a health at a dinner lifts their drink and speaks.

clue.text: Sinister, nothing less, when love is blocked

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: the word for less is blocked by the letter put in its way, sitting inside it

parts.note: minus means less
love is zero in tennis, shown as O

explanation.surface: Menacing indeed, with nothing left once romance is thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is a link word; 'is blocked' puts love's O inside MINUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something threatening suggests harm to come, so a dark menacing quality.

clue.text: New software giving improved exam performance

parts.note: up means improved, as in profits being up
a grade is the mark for an exam

explanation.surface: A better test result thanks to a new computer program.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A later, better version of a program is an improved release.

clue.text: Became popular, like pussy in the rhyme?

definitions.meaning: in 'Ding Dong Bell' the cat is in the well

explanation.surface: Gained favour, like the cat in the nursery verse.
explanation.walkthrough: In the English nursery rhyme 'Ding Dong Bell', pussy has fallen into a well.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-received act was a success, and the nursery cat literally fell down into a well.
